title: Norman the Clairvoyant
scope: Claim-level traceability review of the article and matching dataset entry. Checked BonJour attribution and publication metadata; the Norman Case IV setup; BonJour's argument and its framing as an objection to simple process reliabilism and broader externalist accounts; the distinction between simple process reliabilism and several later responses; qualifications about internalism, externalism, knowledge and justification; the Gettier comparison; the Mr. Truetemp relationship; explicitly editorial teaching framing; and article/dataset metadata reconciliation. This status records traceability of the revised article, not the truth or success of BonJour's argument, a consensus view, an exhaustive survey of reliabilist theories, or expert review.
summary: The revised article preserves BonJour's stipulated Norman scenario and his perspective-based objection, but no longer presents the case as automatically decisive against every reliabilist or externalist theory. It distinguishes the challenge to the sufficiency of simple process reliability from different published replies, qualifies the internalism/externalism framing, and identifies Mr. Truetemp and the thermometer comparison as related-but-distinct case and editorial analogy. Relevant passages in BonJour's primary text, two SEP entries, the IEP reliabilism entry, and the SEP knowledge-analysis entry were read. The publisher's record verifies the article's publication details. The proposed data patch's five reference URLs and their order match the revised Further Reading section exactly; the dataset date is updated to 2026-11-01.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Norman has, under normally obtaining conditions, a completely reliable clairvoyant faculty for certain subject matters; he has no reasons or evidence for or against the power or his possession of it; he forms a true belief that the President is in New York City through that faculty.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Case IV, printed p. 62; corroborated by Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Reliabilist Epistemology,” §2.1.
claim_evidence.finding: The revised scenario closely tracks BonJour's stipulated Case IV and does not treat clairvoyance as an actual-world claim.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a hypothetical stipulation in a philosophical argument, not testimony that clairvoyance exists.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: retained the case's key assumptions, and clarified that the scenario is stipulated rather than asserted as fact.

claim_evidence.material_claim: BonJour argues that Norman's belief is epistemically irrational or unjustified from Norman's own perspective, despite the stipulated truth and reliability.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Printed pp. 62–64, especially BonJour's argument that Norman lacks a reason to treat the belief as having a reliable source and is epistemically irresponsible; see also pp. 65–67 for the broader argumentative framing and possible replies.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text supports the attribution to BonJour. The revised article marks this as BonJour's argument and uses perspective-based framing, rather than reporting it as a settled verdict.
claim_evidence.limitation: A primary philosophical argument establishes what BonJour argues, not that his conclusion is correct. The scanned PDF text has OCR artifacts.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: attributed the irrationality/irresponsibility judgment to BonJour and identified the conclusion as his argument.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Norman is used to challenge the sufficiency of simple process reliability for justification, but the case does not automatically refute every theory that gives reliability a role.
claim_evidence.source_title: Reliabilist Epistemology; Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions of Epistemic Justification
claim_evidence.exact_location: Reliabilist Epistemology §2.1 frames Norman as the clairvoyance problem for process reliabilism and presents different responses; Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions §§1 and 2.1 distinguishes justification and knowledge debates and states that BonJour's intuitions challenge pure externalism, not a wide range of possible externalist views.
claim_evidence.finding: The two reference works support distinguishing the standard process-reliabilist challenge from a blanket conclusion about all reliabilist or externalist theories. BonJour's own paper frames his conclusion more broadly as a challenge to externalist justification; the revised article notes this broader original framing separately.
claim_evidence.limitation: These are secondary syntheses and do not resolve whether a particular reliabilist variant succeeds.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: narrowed the article's claim about the case's reach and retained a sentence describing BonJour's broader original challenge.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The article defines the simple process-reliabilist target as the claim that a belief is justified when produced by a sufficiently reliable process.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1.2 on process reliability and justification, and §2.1 on the clairvoyance problem.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP discussion supports the simplified characterization as pedagogical shorthand for the simple process-reliabilist claim at issue.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article presents a concise teaching formulation, not a complete formal definition of every process-reliabilist theory.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: expressly labels the account 'simple process reliabilism' and avoids generalizing it to every reliabilist view.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Published responses to Norman differ: some defend an externalist verdict, some deny that their theory entails justification in the case, and some introduce additional conditions; examples include approved-list, primal-system, and evidentialist–reliabilist approaches.
claim_evidence.source_title: Reliabilist Epistemology; Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions of Epistemic Justification; Reliabilism
claim_evidence.exact_location: Reliabilist Epistemology §2.1 (approved-list reliabilism and primal systems), §4.2 (evidentialist–reliabilist hybrids); Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions §2.1 (defend Norman's justification, deny entailment, or combine internal/external conditions); IEP Reliabilism §3(a) (Goldman's and other approaches).
claim_evidence.finding: The sources support presenting the replies as distinct strategies rather than as a single reliabilist answer. The revised article uses illustrative categories and does not claim the list is exhaustive.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP and IEP sections survey selected responses; no exhaustive review of the literature or adjudication of each proposal was undertaken.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the compressed 'reliabilists reply' account with a non-exhaustive, differentiated summary.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Internalism/externalism is a broad framing, with differing conceptions of accessibility and external dependence; some views combine internal and external conditions, and philosophers disagree about whether justification/rationality is required for knowledge.
claim_evidence.source_title: Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions of Epistemic Justification
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1 on internal/external and justification/knowledge distinctions; §2.1 on mixed internal and external conditions and lack of consensus about knowledge requiring rational belief or justification.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP passage directly supports the qualifications added to the article's binary framing.
claim_evidence.limitation: The entry is a scholarly overview; the article's one-paragraph summary cannot represent the full range of positions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: identified accessibilism specifically, acknowledged mixed theories, and stated that the justification/knowledge relationship is disputed.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Norman case differs from standard Gettier cases: Gettier cases are commonly presented as justified true beliefs that still appear not to be knowledge due to epistemic luck, whereas Norman challenges whether his belief is justified given lack of reason to trust its source.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Analysis of Knowledge; Externalist Theories of Empirical Knowledge
claim_evidence.exact_location: SEP The Analysis of Knowledge §3 on Gettier cases, justified true belief and epistemic luck; BonJour, Case IV, pp. 62–64, on the Norman justification objection.
claim_evidence.finding: The comparison is supported as a contrast between the standard focus of Gettier cases and BonJour's stated Norman objection. The revised article expressly presents it as a teaching contrast and allows that related questions about knowledge may arise.
claim_evidence.limitation: The contrast is a simplification for readers; the article does not claim that all Gettier cases share one precise diagnosis or that the problems are unrelated.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the contrast and labeled it as teaching framing.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp is a related but distinct example in which reliable temperature beliefs arise from an implanted thermometer-like device without the subject's knowledge of that source.
claim_evidence.exact_location: IEP §3(a), account of Mr. Truetemp and the tempucomp, alongside the Norman discussion; the entry attributes the example to Keith Lehrer (1990).
claim_evidence.finding: The entry describes the distinct device-and-temperature setup and explicitly calls it a similar case. The article now preserves that relationship without equating the cases.
claim_evidence.limitation: Lehrer's original book was not accessed; the attribution and scenario detail are supported here by a scholarly reference-work account.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: described Truetemp as related but distinct and noted that the original case differs in its details.
